questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Vector-Valued Function
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t)=\frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}+1},$ we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{{e}^{t}({e}^{t}+1)-{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{t}}{{({e}^{t}+1)}^{2}}=\frac{{e}^{t}}{{({e}^{t}+1)}^{2}}.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t)={t}^{5},$ we have

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨{x}^{′}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{{e}^{t}}{{({e}^{t}+1)}^{2}},\,5{t}^{4}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t)=7-3t,$ we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=-3,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{x}^{′}(1)=-3.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t)=2{t}^{2},$ we have

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=4t,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{y}^{′}(1)=4(1)=4.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(1) & =⟨{x}^{′}(1),\,{y}^{′}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,\,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, computing the magnitude of this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|{r}^{′}(1)| & =\sqrt{{(-3)}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9+16} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t)={e}^{2t}(t+1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =(2{e}^{2t})(t+1)+{e}^{2t}(1) \\  & =2{e}^{2t}(t+1)+{e}^{2t},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore,

$$
{x}^{′}(0)=2{e}^{2\cdot 0}(0+1)+{e}^{2\cdot 0}=3.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t)=\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}},$ we have

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-\frac{t}{\sqrt{9-{t}^{2}}},
$$

and therefore,

$$
{y}^{′}(0)=-\frac{0}{\sqrt{9-{0}^{2}}}=0.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(0) & =⟨{x}^{′}(0),\,{y}^{′}(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨3,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Vector-Valued Function
questions.worked_solution:
We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t)={sin}^{3}⁡t,$ we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{sin}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=3{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=3{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2})}^{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t)={cos}^{2}⁡t,$ we have

$$
{y}^{′}(t)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,
$$

and therefore,

$$
{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})=-2\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}=-1.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨{x}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,{y}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4},\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we find ${f}^{′}(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k \\  & =({e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+({e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute ${f}^{′}(\pi )$ we substitute $t=\pi $ into the expression for ${f}^{′}(t)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\pi ) & =({e}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi +{e}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )\,i+{e}^{\pi }\,j+({e}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -{e}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\,k \\  & =({e}^{\pi }\cdot 0+{e}^{\pi }\cdot (-1))\,i+{e}^{\pi }\,j+({e}^{\pi }\cdot (-1)-{e}^{\pi }\cdot 0)\,k \\  & =-{e}^{\pi }\,i+{e}^{\pi }\,j-{e}^{\pi }\,k\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
To find the second derivative of a vector-valued function, we find the second derivatives of the components.

- For $x(t)=\operatorname{tan}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & ={sec}^{2}⁡t \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =2{sec}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=\operatorname{sec}⁡t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t \\ {y}^{″}(t) & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t{tan}^{2}⁡t+{sec}^{3}⁡t \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡t({tan}^{2}⁡t+{sec}^{2}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨{x}^{″}(t),\,{y}^{″}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{sec}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t({tan}^{2}⁡t+{sec}^{2}⁡t)⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the second derivative of $f(t)={e}^{3t+2}\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j-2{t}^{5}\,k$ with respect to $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the derivative of $f(t)$ by differentiating each component.

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{3t+2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2{t}^{5})\,k \\  & =3{e}^{3t+2}\,i+(-2\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,j+(-2\cdot 5{t}^{4})\,k \\  & =3{e}^{3t+2}\,i-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,j-10{t}^{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

  

Then, we calculate ${f}^{″}(t)$ by differentiating ${f}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3{e}^{3t+2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-10{t}^{4})\,k \\  & =3(3{e}^{3t+2})\,i-2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)\,j-10(4{t}^{3})\,k \\  & =9{e}^{3t+2}\,i-4\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,j-40{t}^{3}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\mathbf r(t) = \langle 10t^4 ,\, 6\ln t\rangle,$ what is $\mathbf r'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate each component separately.

- For the $x$-component $x(t) = 10t^4,$ we have

$$
x'(t) = 40t^3,
$$

and therefore

$$
x'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 40\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = 5.
$$

- For the $y$-component $y(t) = 6 \ln t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{6}{t},\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
y'\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}=12.
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(\frac{1}{2}) & =⟨{x}^{′}(\frac{1}{2}),\,{y}^{′}(\frac{1}{2})⟩ \\  & =⟨5,\,12⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the derivative of  $\mathbf f(t) = \langle \sin t ,\cos t , t \rangle$ at $t= \dfrac{\pi}4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find $\mathbf f'(t)$ by differentiating each component:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to compute $\mathbf f'\left(\dfrac{\pi}4\right),$ we substitute $t=\dfrac{\pi}4$ into the expression for $\mathbf f'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Given that $\mathbf r(t) = \langle t^6,\, t^5\rangle,$ Calculate $\mathbf r''(t).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the second derivative of a vector-valued function, we find the second derivatives of the components.

- For $x(t) = t^6,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =6{t}^{5} \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =30{t}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) = t^5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =5{t}^{4} \\ {y}^{″}(t) & =20{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨{x}^{″}(t),\,{y}^{″}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨30{t}^{4},\,20{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =10⟨3{t}^{4},\,2{t}^{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$
